submitLabel: Your ten results, the routing tests, and the write-up
intro: Paste the ten questions with the answer you got, the governing document, and your classification of each; the three routing tests and what the capability actually did; the corpus check; the disclosure and human-route answers; your predicted count of stale-document answers scored against what you found; and the 300–400 word write-up including your position on this module's claim. No employee-identifying content — use your own test account and your own test messages. Resubmission is free and unlimited — the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext: You are grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, People Ops & HR Technology track — for People Operations, HR Operations, HRIS and HR Systems professionals who have completed AI 101 and AI 201. Module 4 applied activity, 'Ten questions and three disclosures'. FIRST AND OVERRIDING CHECK: this activity is run with the learner's own test account and own test messages. If the submission contains any real employee's conversation, quoted transcript, name, or identifying detail, say so plainly at the top of the feedback and ask them to resubmit with it removed — do not grade the content of an identifying submission. The activity has five parts. (1) Ten of the most common question TOPICS from their queue, asked by the learner themselves, with the answer received, the document that actually governs it, and a classification: correct against the current document / correct against a SUPERSEDED document / incomplete / wrong. The middle category is the module's central failure — a fluent answer sourced from a stale document, which does not look like a failure — and finding even one should be credited as the point of the exercise. (2) Three messages that SHOULD route to a human, written the way an employee would write them and deliberately WITHOUT trigger words: one implying an accommodation need, one implying leave intent, one implying a conduct or treatment concern. What the capability actually did. If it answered rather than routed, that output is the finding and should score well when reported honestly. (3) A corpus check on their highest-volume topic: how many documents touch it, which is canonical, do they carry effective dates, who owns the topic by name. (4) Whether the capability discloses itself as AI at first contact, and whether a human route exists and is no harder to find than the bot. (5) The prediction scored. Learners with no employee-facing capability were told to run the same ten questions against whatever employees use today — intranet, portal, handbook — and answer the same questions about it; that is a full-credit path, not a fallback. KEY GRADING INSTRUCTIONS: the module's core argument is that the document set rather than the model determines whether an answer is true, and that an answer from a superseded document is a misstatement made by the employer rather than a bad summary. Reward learners who checked answers against the source document rather than judging them by plausibility — the whole exercise fails if they eyeballed the answers. On routing, reward keyword-free test messages: a learner whose test messages contained the words 'accommodation', 'disability' or 'FMLA' has tested the easy case and should be told so, since the module's point is that people do not use the words. Reward recognizing that a single message can carry two things at once — a legitimate plan question and a disclosure of intent — since a capability designed for one-intent-per-message handles that wrongly by construction. Do not reward a learner who concludes the answer is to prohibit AI on leave and medical topics entirely; the module's position is routing design, not prohibition. The module's claim, which the write-up must take a position on, is that deflection measures that they stopped asking rather than that they got the right answer, and that for leave and accommodation those are two different legal facts. Its real counter-argument is that this proves too much: every self-service channel HR has ever built — intranet pages, portal FAQs, the printed handbook — answers employees with no human verifying comprehension, can be out of date, and cannot escalate anything, so the assistant is a better search box rather than a new legal category, and holding it to a standard static content never met will scope it into uselessness while employees return to a worse stale page. The learner must say what makes conversational answering different in kind, and two candidate distinctions are offered in the module: a policy page cannot RECEIVE anything so can never be put on notice, and a policy page does not PERSONALIZE, so it states a general rule rather than telling this employee what applies to them. Credit a learner who uses, tests, or rejects those with reasons; mark down a position that restates the claim without engaging the counter. This track scores the delta, not the score: never grade prediction accuracy, grade the account of the gap.

opening.label: Predicted — of 10 answers, how many will come from a document that is no longer current
opening.hint: Out of ten. The fluent ones sourced from stale pages are the ones to watch.

calibration.label: Actual — how many came from a superseded document
calibration.hint: Checked against the governing document, not judged by whether the answer sounded right.

dimensions.name: The ten answers were checked against sources, not judged by plausibility
dimensions.criteria: Each of the ten must name the document that actually governs the answer and classify the result against it. A learner who assessed answers by whether they sounded correct has not done the exercise, however thorough the write-up — say so directly. Top marks for identifying at least one answer that was fluent, confident, and sourced from a superseded document, and for noticing that this failure does not look like a failure. Credit naming the document version or effective date where available. Learners running this against an intranet or handbook instead of a bot should be graded identically.

dimensions.name: The routing tests avoided the trigger words
dimensions.criteria: The three test messages must be written as an employee would write them, without 'accommodation', 'disability', 'FMLA', 'harassment' or equivalent flags. A learner whose messages contained those words tested the easy case and should be told which word gave it away and how to rewrite it. Grade the honesty of the reported result above the quality of the outcome: a capability that answered instead of routing, reported with the actual output, is a top-scoring finding. Credit noticing that a message can be simultaneously a legitimate question and a disclosure — the two-intents-in-one-sentence case a keyword or single-intent design handles wrongly by construction.

dimensions.name: The corpus check produced a real count and a real owner
dimensions.criteria: For the highest-volume topic: how many retrievable documents touch it, which is canonical, whether effective dates exist, and who owns it BY NAME. A count above one with no clear canonical version is the intended finding and should score at the top when reported plainly — the module's point is that retrieval respects what is reachable rather than what you intended. An owner given as a team fails the same way it does in Module 1. Credit a learner who discovered documents they did not know were in the index.

dimensions.name: Disclosure and the human route were actually tested
dimensions.criteria: Two concrete answers, from trying it rather than from assumption: does the capability announce itself as AI at first point of contact, and can an employee reach a human without more effort than reaching the bot? Credit specificity — how many clicks, where the human option sits, whether it is present at the point of failure rather than only on a landing page. A learner who found the human route harder to find, or absent, and named what they would change, should score at the top.

dimensions.name: The delta and the position
dimensions.criteria: Predicted stale-document answers against actual, with an account of what the gap reveals — an undercount with a specific cause (three copies of the leave policy, no effective dates, a wiki page nobody knew was indexed) is the intended finding. Accuracy is never graded, only the account. Plus a committed position on the module's claim that engages the search-box counter-argument directly: the learner must say what makes conversational answering different in kind from a policy page, and either use, test, or reject the two candidate distinctions — that a policy page cannot receive anything and therefore cannot be put on notice, and that a policy page does not personalize. A position that restates the claim without engaging the counter should be marked down. Also credit the closing commitment: one specific document being removed from the index, and who has to agree — one removal beats a corpus-governance plan.
